Research / Minerva 22 September 2026

Finding hidden
biology with AI

A genome language model can reveal relationships that are easy to miss in a string of genetic letters. Minerva turns those clues into a starting point for discovery.

Research by David B. Li, Garyk Brixi and colleagues ↗

A genome is more than a collection of recipes for making proteins. Some of its most interesting stretches encode RNA molecules that fold into shapes, interact with other molecules, and help cells regulate their genes. Many of these regions still have no known function.

Finding them is difficult when the search begins with something already familiar. Related RNA molecules can change their genetic letters while preserving their shape. A search for matching sequences can overlook that deeper resemblance.

Minerva looks for interactions between positions in a genome. It uses patterns learned by an AI model to predict which letters may pair, which regions belong to repeated motifs, and which amino acids may contact one another. The result is a map that helps scientists decide where to look and what to test.

An interactive guide

From an RNA molecule to a map

RNA is a chain of letters called nucleotides. When parts of the chain pair, they can form a stem topped by a loop, called a hairpin. Follow those pairs into a grid, then reveal the repeats.

A folded strand

Two copies of an illustrative RNA hairpin motif

The same relationships, in a grid

Both axes follow the same strand, from 5′ to 3′

Base pair · physical pairingRepeat · corresponding positionsSame position

If base 1 pairs with base 14, mark row 1, column 14—and its mirror, row 14, column 1. A hairpin’s two sides run in opposite directions, producing a short line across the diagonal.

Corresponding positions in direct repeats advance in the same direction, creating lines parallel to the diagonal. Those purple marks do not mean the two bases physically touch.

Teaching schematic, not model output or a folding simulation. These two identical toy motifs have assumed A–U and G–C pairs; real RNAs can include G–U and other pairings, bulges, and more complex folds. This is a base-pair map, not a complete map of 3D distances. In the paper, Minerva predicts graded interaction scores directly from sequence.

01 / Learning what is preserved by evolution

The letters change, the interactions can remain.

Imagine two positions that pair in an RNA stem. Over evolution, a change at one position can be accompanied by a change at the other that preserves pairing. The exact letters differ, but the interaction survives.

Traditionally, scientists look for such coordinated changes by lining up many related sequences. Instead, Minerva starts with a genome language model trained to fill in missing parts of microbial sequences. To make good predictions, the model can learn dependencies between positions, including signals consistent with the constraints that evolution preserves.

We developed two ways to read out these dependencies. One changes letters in the computer and measures how the model’s other predictions respond. The faster approach combines internal model signals into specialized predictors for base pairing, repeats, and protein contacts. These predictors are trained on a small set of labeled examples.

What “alignment-free” means here

Minerva can predict a map for a new input without first building a multiple sequence alignment for that input. The study still uses alignments and covariance models later to examine and search for candidate RNA families. Its underlying Minerva-MLM model was continued from gLM2 with a trillion additional training tokens; it represents annotated coding regions as amino acids and intergenic regions as DNA. So “genome language model” does not mean that every input token is a DNA base.

02 / Looking across whole genomes

A way to find new genetic elements

Speed changes the kind of question scientists can ask. Instead of examining only a few familiar regions, we used Minerva’s fast predictors to scan 150 bacterial genomes in 100 minutes on a single H100 GPU.

The scan picked up expected landmarks, such as strong repeat signals around CRISPR arrays and strong base-pairing signals around ribosomal RNAs. It also flagged many regions outside existing annotations.

40,175unannotated candidate loci with
at least two predicted hairpins

Of 57,787 loci predicted to contain at least two neighboring hairpins, 40,175 (69.5%) fell outside existing annotations. Each counted hairpin had a predicted stem of at least five base pairs. With a stricter requirement of four hairpins, the study found 9,044 loci, of which 41.1% were unannotated.

The scan creates a more informed starting set for follow-up. Two examples show what that follow-up can reveal.

03 / Seeing more of a familiar RNA

Extending a known RNA family

One lead came from an RNA family called TwoAYGGAY, named for a short sequence pattern in its loops. Existing annotations captured a recognizable core. Minerva predicted that, in some bacteria, the RNA’s structure extended well beyond that core.

Further sequence comparisons supported an extended architecture with additional hairpins and a pseudoknot, a pairing arrangement that cannot be drawn using only neatly nested arcs. The larger architecture was concentrated in the broad bacterial group Pseudomonadota; it was not a universal feature of the family.

We used these predictions to improve a conventional search model. That model found 16,086 matches in 1,148 Pseudomonas strains. AI suggested a relationship that made established comparative methods more effective.

04 / From an unexpected pattern to an experiment

Different sequences, a shared architecture

A second lead appeared near genes for a little-understood group of enzymes called UG27 reverse transcriptases. A reverse transcriptase copies information from RNA into DNA. But what RNA did these particular systems copy?

Minerva highlighted arrays of neighboring RNA units with similar predicted structures, even though their sequences were quite different. The pattern was difficult to recognize in a conventional sequence dotplot. Additional training on related UG27 regions sharpened the structural predictions and helped us align the units.

The five systems identified in the initial genome collection lay within prophages, bacteriophage genomes integrated into bacterial DNA. Broader searches showed that the arrays vary in their number of RNA units and in their sequences, while retaining a common predicted architecture.

Lab experiments supplied the answer

The crucial next step happened in the lab. When we expressed the five UG27 systems in E. coli, all five produced short, single-stranded DNA products, roughly 50–100 nucleotides long. Sequencing showed that the products corresponded to central hairpins in the RNA units.

Controls connected this output to the system’s machinery: disabling reverse-transcriptase activity eliminated the products. In two tested systems, removing either of the two accessory proteins also eliminated production.

UG27 systems can use the RNA array as a template to make short DNA products. The DNA products are themselves predicted to fold into hairpins. Their shapes have not been established experimentally in this study, and what the products do in their native biological setting remains unknown.

05 / What this changes

A discovery engine for biology

Minerva illustrates a practical way AI can accelerate discovery. A model learns from a large body of biological sequences, then we turn its internal patterns into interpretable predictions, use those predictions to prioritize unfamiliar regions, and design experiments to find out what is happening.

There are still limitations to the current approaches that provide fruitful ground for future work. Minerva sees a bounded stretch of sequence at a time, so it can miss distant relationships. It predicts protein contacts less accurately than a specialized protein model in the study’s benchmark, and RNA–protein interactions remain difficult. Additional training can strengthen one type of signal while weakening another. Predicted structure alone does not establish function.

The opportunity is to turn more of the sequence data we already have into questions we can test. Minerva shows one route from a pattern learned by AI to a biological finding.
